tagline: Over the mountain on gravel, the way the turnpike went.
intro: Out of Beverly, the oldest settlement in the Tygart Valley, Rich Mountain Road climbs west on the line of the old Staunton-Parkersburg Turnpike. About five miles over the mountain are still gravel, twisting with the contour at a 19th-century pace. At the top of the pass is the battlefield. Then the road drops past Camp Garnett and runs out through Mabie toward Coalton.
The fight up here on July 11, 1861 gave the Union its hold on western Virginia for most of the war, the first step toward a separate West Virginia.

moments.title: Rich Mountain Battlefield
moments.text: A local boy, David Hart, led a Union brigade around through the woods for an offered hundred dollars in gold, and the fighting came down on his own family's farm.

moments.title: Camp Garnett
moments.text: A mile and a half down the west side, trails lead to the earthworks of the Confederate camp that held the turnpike in the early summer of 1861.

moments.title: Mabie
moments.text: The rolling ground along Roaring Creek was the Union camp the attack set out from, beside a town later renamed for W. H. Mabie, who built a sawmill there in 1897.

practical: About five miles over the mountain are gravel, twisting with the contour.
